tagline: A highway brought to the lakeshore, linking beaches and small communities
intro: US 2 follows Lake Michigan through Naubinway, crosses the Cut River high above its valley, and passes through Hiawatha National Forest near Brevort. The Top of the Lake route belongs to the Pure Michigan Byways program. The Eastern Upper Peninsula Regional Planning and Development Commission highlights its white-sand beaches, views and small communities between St. Ignace and Manistique.

The highway did not always keep so close to the water. In 1936, the Michigan State Highway Department began a new lakeshore road into St. Ignace, replacing an inland routing from Brevort through Moran. In 1941, another realignment carried US 2 from Gould City through Naubinway and along the lake to Epoufette. The new highway initially detoured around Cut River, where steel shortages during World War II delayed the bridge. Completion came after the war.

Driving west from St. Ignace, follow the shore toward Brevort, where Lake Michigan and Brevoort Lake flank the road. Cross the Cut River before Epoufette and continue through Naubinway; US 2 then passes south of Engadine and heads inland past Gould City to Blaney Park. Beyond Gulliver, the road returns to Lake Michigan at Manistique and crosses the river that gives the city its name.

moments.title: Cut River Bridge
moments.text: Cut River Bridge carries US 2 across a valley 147 feet below the roadway. The State Highway Department designed the crossing, and W.J. Meagher and Sons began construction in 1941. Wartime demand for steel halted work until after World War II. The finished cantilever spans 641 feet and contains 888 short tons of structural steel. A wooden staircase was added later to reach the valley. Under the east end, an office door bears a brass plaque inscribed “T. Troll.” Original metal guardrails remain on the sidewalks on both sides of the roadway.
moments.notice: The sidewalk guardrails are original; the steel members have extensive latticing.

moments.title: Naubinway
moments.text: Lake Michigan supplied Naubinway with both a harbor and a place on a territorial boundary. The lake’s northernmost point helped define the western boundary of Michigan Territory in 1805; the territory expanded westward in 1818. By 1880, Naubinway was a lumbering community, with commercial fishing growing alongside the timber trade. Fishing continued after lumber declined at the turn of the century. Millecoquins Point forms the natural harbor, which contains a park and marina. US 2 was rerouted through the community along Lake Michigan beginning in the 1940s, providing a major transportation route.

moments.title: Manistique
moments.text: Manistique takes its name from its river, but not its original spelling. The river was spelled Monistique; a mistake in the city charter produced the name used now. At the river mouth, a natural harbor has been improved with dredging, breakwaters and the Manistique East Breakwater Light. Timber and pig iron shipped daily from this harbor at the beginning of the twentieth century. The east light first shone on August 17, 1916, after completion of the east breakwater the previous year. Its square tower is assembled from prefabricated steel plates bolted together.
